prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Come live with me, and be my love, And we will some new pleasures prove Of golden sands, and crystal brooks, With silken lines, and silver hooks. There will the river whispering run Warm'd by thy eyes, more than the sun; And there the 'enamour'd fish will stay, Begging themselves they may betray. When thou wilt swim in that live bath, Each fish, which every channel hath, Will amorously to thee swim, Gladder to catch thee, than thou him. If thou, to be so seen, be'st loth, By sun or moon, thou dark'nest both, And if myself have leave to see, I need not their light having thee. Let others freeze with angling reeds, And cut their legs with shells and weeds, Or treacherously poor fish beset, With strangling snare, or windowy net. Let coarse bold hands from slimy nest The bedded fish in banks out-wrest; Or curious traitors, sleeve-silk flies, Bewitch poor fishes' wand'ring eyes. For thee, thou need'st no such deceit, For thou thyself art thine own bait: That fish, that is not catch'd thereby, Alas, is wiser far than I.

outputs.L2:
Come share your life with me as my beloved, and together we will discover unfamiliar delights among shining beaches and clear-flowing streams, using threads of silk and hooks of silver. The river will murmur as it passes, heated more by the radiance of your gaze than by sunlight. Captivated fish will linger there, almost pleading to surrender themselves.

Whenever you enter that living pool to bathe, fish from every waterway will eagerly approach you, more delighted at the thought of capturing you than you could be of catching them. If you dislike being watched while swimming, your beauty will eclipse both sun and moon. And if I alone am permitted to look upon you, their illumination will be unnecessary, because your presence will provide all the light I need.

Others may shiver while fishing with rods, injuring their legs on sharp shells and tangled plants. They may ambush helpless fish with suffocating traps or transparent nets. Rough, fearless hands may drag hidden fish from their muddy shelters along the banks, while cunning fishermen deceive their roaming eyes with artificial flies fashioned from silk.

You, however, require none of these tricks, because your own beauty serves as the lure. Any fish that cannot be caught by such bait must, sadly, possess far greater wisdom than I do.
outputs.L3:
The speaker invites his beloved to come and live with him in an idyllic natural setting, where they can enjoy simple pleasures beside golden sands and clear, sparkling brooks. In his vision, the landscape is transformed by her presence: her beauty gives the river more warmth and light than either the sun or the moon could provide.

Even the fish are captivated by her. Enchanted by her beauty, they willingly swim toward her and seem more eager to be caught than she is to catch them. Unlike ordinary anglers, who must rely on cruel or deceptive devices—traps, nets, hooks, and artificial flies—she has no need for such methods. Her presence alone is enough to draw the fish near.

The beloved is therefore presented as irresistible bait in her own right. Any fish capable of resisting her charms, the speaker concludes, must possess greater wisdom and self-control than he does, for he is already completely overcome by love.
outputs.L4: The speaker invites his beloved to join him in an idyllic life beside a peaceful river, where they can enjoy the beauty and pleasures of the natural world together. He imagines clear streams, warm sunshine, and schools of fish moving through the water, transforming the riverside into an ideal setting for love. Throughout the poem, he develops an elaborate fishing metaphor in which the woman herself becomes the most powerful “bait.” Her radiant beauty is so captivating that the fish willingly swim toward her, enchanted by her presence rather than attracted by hooks, flies, or other artificial lures. Even the speaker presents himself as one of those helplessly fascinated creatures, willingly caught by her charms. By concluding that she has no need of conventional bait, he emphasizes the irresistible power of her natural allure. The imagery therefore expresses both his admiration and his surrender: he is wholly devoted to her and gladly accepts love as a form of captivity.

### Come, And, With

Come—not because the road is easy, but because it is waiting.

Bring your hopes, your questions, and the quiet courage you thought you had lost. We will walk beyond the familiar, where every turn offers a new beginning.

Come with me, and we will face the distance together. For even the longest journey feels lighter when it is shared.

counterfactuals.output:
## “The Bait”  
**John Donne**

Come live with me, and be my love,  
And we will some new pleasures prove  
Of golden sands and crystal brooks,  
With silken lines and silver hooks.

There will the river whispering run,  
Warm’d by thy eyes, more than the sun;  
And there th’ enamour’d fish will stay,  
Begging themselves they may betray.

When thou wilt swim in that live bath,  
Each fish, which every channel hath,  
Will amorously to thee swim,  
Gladder to catch thee, than thou him.

If thou, to be so seen, be’st loth,  
By sun or moon, thou darkenest both,  
And if myself have leave to see,  
I need not their light, having thee.

Let others freeze with angling reeds,  
And cut their legs with shells and weeds,  
Or treacherously poor fish beset,  
With strangling snare, or windowy net.

Let coarse bold hands from slimy nest  
The bedded fish in banks out-wrest,  
Or curious traitors, sleeve-silk flies,  
Bewitch poor fishes’ wandering eyes.

For thee, thou need’st no such deceit,  
For thou thyself art thine own bait;  
That fish, that is not catch’d thereby,  
Alas, is wiser far than I.
